name: Nora Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a workday involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and lead a small opera chorus, sing a solo now and then, record audition examples and coach younger singers. I have a master’s in music and can hear a singer pressing before the voice breaks. I like the quiet minute when the chorus finds a shared breath, but the unpaid messages about recording reuse wear me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How secure is that work at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner keeps books for a furniture shop, our children are grown, and the mortgage still runs. My opera and coaching pay is fairly typical, we have five months of expenses saved, and a few other choirs work nearby. I use AI daily to sort my own audition clips, then listen to every cut and keep students’ voices out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the chorus that a quicker call list is fine if the solo, coaching and rehearsal fees remain beside each date. I would ask the manager to sign recording-use terms as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This season is paid and five months saved covers an ordinary gap between productions. The mortgage is not gone, but the current chorus and private coaching hours give us a workable year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep the booked opera rehearsals and six coaching pupils, and request written fees for repeat use of my audition recordings. In the plateau’s first year I would ask for an actual pension estimate and set the figure beside our mortgage and health before choosing any retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the current run. A singer’s voice can be used twice, but the second use still needs a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is repeat use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A producer can put one recorded audition example in a later class. I want that later use named and paid in the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the estimate decide when you stop singing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I would compare the actual amount with bills and the work I can still do. We have no date set.

I would ask for **signed recording-use terms**.
think: Our **five-month reserve** handles a normal gap between opera productions without forcing us to miss mortgage bills.
The **current chorus and pupils** provide paid hours that cover this season’s household costs.

Request an **actual pension estimate** in the plateau’s first year and compare it with mortgage and health.
feel: I feel **calm** about paid work this season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the opera manager that generated audition examples could save time, but the chorus still needs a paid human to hear breath and balance. I would ask which recording-use and coaching hours remain paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reused audition examples bring about one day’s fee each month, and I expect some producers to make their own with software. The five-month cushion buys time, but I would notice a recurring day missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would take last season’s reuse invoices to the manager and request a written fee for each new use and paid coaching hour. In disruption’s first year I would continue my own daily clip sorting, but I would keep pupils’ names and voices out of it and compare each cut with the original before sharing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic loss of those monthly reuse fees. My strongest skill is hearing a living chorus, and I need that work to be paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you use a generated voice in a pupil lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask permission before using any learner recording. My own clips are enough to check a lesson example.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager calls reuse publicity?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the actual fee in writing before saying yes. Publicity is not a paid coaching hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the chorus that thinking AGI in 2028 could make audition examples before a robot could sing beside us around 2031. I would ask for the paid live chorus dates in writing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the audition-example reuse fees to end in 2028, and some planning calls may go too. The live coaching is still booked, so I will not count a whole job loss before the calendar changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would total reuse and planning invoices and ask for signed chorus and pupil hours. In the first year after 2028, if the example fees end and paid live coaching also falls, I would apply for a posted paid conservatory vocal-coach role only if it accepts my music master’s and chorus-leading record, pays for face-to-face voice work, offers written net pay after travel replacing lost income and has an evening train home; I would keep current opera and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the likely loss of a paid day each month and possible planning calls. Five months saved lets me check real vacancies rather than leave a booked chorus on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a human vocal coach still do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would hear the first hint of strain and stop a singer before an injury. I have done that in rehearsal, but a conservatory must actually post and pay for the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why distinguish robots from the 2028 change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card puts capable singing robots around 2031. A producer can stop paying for a file in 2028 without one.

I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from robot singers around 2031.

Seek **posted paid vocal coach** after BOTH reuse/live losses if master’s/leadership qualify; require paid face-to-face work, replacement net after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the chorus that five years until AGI by 2031 gives us time to write down which live coaching hours a school will buy. Singing robots around 2034 are a later issue than a signed rehearsal call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Audition files may lose their fee over five years, but the opera’s live chorus remains booked for now. I could use the runway to secure a longer paid coaching term instead of buying an unneeded qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would propose a two-year written opera coaching term that pays for live chorus rehearsal, individual voice checks and preparation. In the first year after 2031 I would keep those paid calls and six pupils if the company signs; if reuse fees and live coaching both fall, I would seek a posted paid conservatory voice-coach role only if it accepts my master’s and chorus leadership, pays face-to-face voice coaching, and written net pay after travel replaces both losses and the evening train fits, keeping current paid work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious that reuse fees may disappear even while the paid live calendar holds. A two-year promise is useful only when it names the paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the company offered the longer term?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would ask for the written hours, not count a plan as a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about a new course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No posted job has asked for another certificate. I would keep paid coaching before spending household money on one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell younger singers that ten years until AGI by 2036 gives time to get recording-use and coaching rates into contracts. Robot singers around 2039 do not settle today’s rehearsal fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want fewer late performances, but I have not seen an actual pension amount. Live singing and pupils pay now, and our five-month reserve gives some space if reuse fees fade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request an actual pension estimate and written opera renewal, then save ten percent of any extra cleared recital fee after mortgage, food and travel toward eight months of bills. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid chorus and pupils while booked; if reuse and live fees both fall, I would apply to a posted paid conservatory vocal-coach role only if my master’s and leadership qualify, face-to-face hours pay, written net pay after travel replaces the loss and the evening train works, staying in current paid work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the later reuse market while current live work covers our bills. An unverified pension is a question for the statement, not a cheque in my hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra recital pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I save nothing new from recitals. Eight months is a target, not money already in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Will you retire when the estimate arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I would compare the actual amount with bills, health and paid offers. We have no date fixed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because recording reuse could stop paying quickly before I secure a longer live term. Signed chorus hours, a real vocal-coach vacancy accepting my master’s and a written net offer after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns a singer’s second use of the same recording. A recorded breath can travel farther than the singer who made it, and the fee should follow.

headlineQuote: A recorded breath can travel farther than the singer who made it, and the fee should follow.
portrait: Nora is a **senior chorus leader** with a music master’s, opera work, audition examples and six pupils.
Her **typical pay**, five-month reserve, mortgage and some nearby choirs make current work fairly steady.
She uses **AI daily** to sort owned audition clips and listens before sharing, while protecting pupil voices.
She seeks **written reuse rights** and paid live coaching, with a posted human role only after actual dual losses.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could end paid audition-example reuse before a longer live term is secured.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **signed chorus hours**, a real vocal-coach vacancy accepting her master’s and written replacement net after travel.
